column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 43: “Give the fixed shares to those entitled to them”

column2: From Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Give the fixed shares (farāʾiḍ) to those entitled to them, and whatever the shares leave over goes to the nearest male relative.”
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded it.

This is the hadith that one of the commentators on these Forty claimed the Shaykh (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) had overlooked, since it covers the rulings of inheritance and brings them together.

The two of them recorded this hadith through the narration of Wuhayb and Rawḥ ibn al-Qāsim, from Ibn Ṭāwūs, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās; and Muslim recorded it through the narration of Maʿmar and Yaḥyā ibn Ayyūb, also from Ibn Ṭāwūs.
Al-Thawrī, Ibn ʿUyaynah, Ibn Jurayj and others narrated it from Ibn Ṭāwūs, from his father, in mursal form, without mention of Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Nasāʾī judged the mursal version the more likely.
The scholars have differed over the meaning of his words, “Give the fixed shares to those entitled to them.”

One group said: The farāʾiḍ meant are the shares specified in the Book of Allah the Exalted, and the meaning is: give the specified shares to those for whom Allah has named them; whatever remains after these shares is due to the nearest (awlā) man.

By awlā is meant the nearest, as when it is said, “This is next to (yalī) that,” meaning near it. The nearest man is the nearest of the agnatic heirs (ʿaṣabah), and he is entitled to the remainder by agnatic right. A number of the imams explained the hadith in this sense,

among them Imam Aḥmad and Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh; Isḥāq ibn Manṣūr transmitted this from them both. On this view, when a daughter, a sister and a paternal uncle — or a paternal uncle's son, or a brother's son — are together,

it is the agnatic heir who should take what remains after the daughter's half. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. He held fast to this hadith, while acknowledging that all the people were against him; and the Ẓāhirīs also adopted his view.
Isḥāq said: If there is an agnatic heir along with the daughter and the sister, the agnatic heir has the better right; if there is no one else with them, the sister takes the remainder.
It is related that Ibn Masʿūd said: The daughter is the agnatic heir of one who has no agnatic heir. Some rejected this, saying that it is not authentically reported from Ibn Masʿūd.
Ibn al-Zubayr and Masrūq used to hold Ibn ʿAbbās's view, and then retracted it.

The majority of scholars hold that the sister, together with the daughter, is an agnatic heir and takes what is left over. Among them are ʿUmar, ʿAlī, ʿĀʾishah, Zayd, Ibn Masʿūd and Muʿādh ibn Jabal, and the rest of the scholars followed them.
ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported: Ibn Jurayj informed us: I asked Ibn Ṭāwūs about a daughter and a sister. He said: My father used to mention something on it from Ibn ʿAbbās,
from a man, from the Prophet ﷺ, and Ṭāwūs was not satisfied with that man. He said: My father was in doubt about it and would say nothing on it, though he used to be asked about it.

It appears — and Allah knows best — that what Ṭāwūs meant is this hadith; for Ibn ʿAbbās had no explicit text from the Prophet ﷺ on the inheritance of the sister alongside the daughter, but only held fast to the general sense of hadiths such as this one.

As for Ṭāwūs's remark that Ibn ʿAbbās narrated it from a man with whom he was not satisfied: most of Ibn ʿAbbās's narrations of hadith are from the Companions, and the Companions are all of upright character; Allah is pleased with them and has praised them, so after that Ṭāwūs's dissatisfaction counts for nothing.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Abū Qays al-Awdī, from Huzayl ibn Shuraḥbīl, who said: A man came to Abū Mūsā

and asked him about a daughter, a son's daughter and a full sister. He said: The daughter has half, and the sister has what remains. Go to Ibn Masʿūd, and he will agree with me. The man went to Ibn Masʿūd and told him that,
and he said: Then I would have gone astray and would not be among the rightly guided! I will judge in it with the judgement of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: the daughter has half,

the son's daughter has a sixth, completing the two-thirds, and what remains goes to the sister. He said: We went to Abū Mūsā and told him what Ibn Masʿūd had said, and he said: Do not ask me anything so long as this learned man is among you.
It also has, from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm, from al-Aswad ibn Yazīd, who said: Muʿādh ibn Jabal judged among us in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: half to the daughter
and half to the sister. Later al-Aʿmash left out the mention of the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and no longer mentioned it.
Abū Dāwūd recorded it by another route from al-Aswad, adding: And the Prophet of Allah ﷺ was alive at that time.

Ibn ʿAbbās argued for his view from the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalālah. If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, she has half of what he left” [al-Nisāʾ 4:176]. He used to say: Do you know better, or Allah?
He meant that Allah gave her half only when there is no child, while you give her half when there is a child, namely the daughter.
The correct view is that of ʿUmar and the majority, and this verse does not indicate otherwise,

because what is meant by His words, “she has half of what he left,” is half as a fixed share, and this is conditional on there being no child at all. That is why He then says: “If there are two sisters, they have two-thirds of what he left” [al-Nisāʾ 4:176], meaning as a fixed share. A single sister takes half only when there is no child, male or female;

likewise two or more sisters are entitled to two-thirds only when there is no child, male or female. If there is a child, then if it is male, he takes precedence over the siblings absolutely, male and female alike;

and if there is no male child but there is a female one, then the remainder after her share goes to the brother together with his sister, by agreement. If the sister is not excluded by her own brother,
how can she be excluded by agnatic heirs more distant than he is, such as the paternal uncle and his son?

And if the more distant agnatic heir does not exclude her, she must take precedence over him, since he cannot share with her. What the verse implies is that a child prevents the sister from having half as a fixed share, and that is true; it does not imply that the sister is excluded by the daughter and does not take what is left over of the estate.

This is shown by His words, Exalted is He: “And he inherits from her if she has no child” [al-Nisāʾ 4:176]. The nation is agreed that a female child does not prevent the brother from inheriting from his sister's estate whatever is left over after the daughter or daughters;

the existence of a female child only prevents the brother from taking his sister's whole estate. Just as a child, if male, prevents the brother from inheriting, and if female does not prevent him from taking what is left over of her estate,

though it prevents him from taking the whole estate, so too a child, if male, prevents the sister from inheriting altogether, and if female, prevents a half from being assigned to the sister as a fixed share but does not prevent her from taking what is left over after the daughter's share. And Allah knows best.

As for his words, “and whatever the shares leave over goes to the nearest male relative,” it has been said that what is meant is specifically the distant agnatic heir, such as brothers' sons, paternal uncles and their sons, and not the near agnatic heir,

the evidence being that the remainder after the fixed shares is shared by male and female when the agnatic heir is near, as with children and siblings, by agreement; and the same holds for the sister with the daughter, by the text that indicates it.

Moreover, these cases are excepted from it by agreement, and likewise the woman who freed the deceased, his patroness (mawlāt al-niʿmah), is excepted from it by agreement; so the case of the sister with the daughter is excepted from it by the text.

Another group said: What is meant by his words, “Give the fixed shares to those entitled to them,” is what those who have fixed shares are entitled to in general, whether they take it as a fixed share or by an agnatic right that arises for them;

and what is meant by his words, “and whatever is left goes to the nearest male relative,” is the agnatic heir who never has a fixed share in any case. This is shown by the fact that the hadith has been narrated with another wording:

“Divide the estate among those entitled to fixed shares according to the Book of Allah.” This includes everyone who is in any way among those entitled to fixed shares. On this view, what the sister takes together with her brother, or with her paternal cousin when he makes her an agnatic heir, falls within this division,
since she is in general among those entitled to fixed shares; and the same is true of what the sister takes together with the daughter.

Another group said: Those entitled to the farāʾiḍ, in his words, “Give the fixed shares to those entitled to them,” and, “Divide the estate among those entitled to fixed shares,” are all the heirs whom Allah has named in His Book, both those with fixed shares and the agnatic heirs;

for everything the heirs take is a share (farḍ) that Allah has allotted (faraḍa) to them, whether specified or not, as He says after mentioning the inheritance of parents and children: “an allotment (farīḍah) from Allah” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11] — and among them are both sharers and agnatic heirs — and as He says:

“For men there is a share of what parents and relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what parents and relatives leave, whether it is little or much — an allotted share” [al-Nisāʾ 4:7]. This includes both the agnatic heirs and those with fixed shares.

Likewise his words, “Divide the shares among those entitled to them according to the Book of Allah,” include dividing the estate among those with fixed shares and the agnatic heirs according to what is in the Book of Allah.

If it is divided accordingly and something of it is left over, the leftover goes specifically to the nearest male among the heirs. Likewise, if the Book of Allah contains nothing explicit about dividing it among the heirs Allah has named, the estate then goes to the nearest male among them.

This hadith, then, explains how the inheritances mentioned in the Book of Allah are to be divided among those entitled to them, and how whatever of the estate is left over from that division is to be divided, in those situations and categories of these heirs that the Qurʾān does not state explicitly.

It also explains how the remaining agnatic heirs, whom the Qurʾān does not explicitly name, inherit. When this hadith is joined to the verses of the Qurʾān, all of it together gives knowledge of how inheritances are divided among all those with fixed shares and the agnatic heirs.

We shall mention the ruling on the inheritance of children and parents, as Allah mentioned it at the beginning of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, and the ruling on the inheritance of full siblings or paternal half-siblings, as Allah mentioned it at the end of that sūrah.

As for children, Allah the Exalted says: “Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, the like of the portion of two females” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11]. This is the ruling when their males and females are together: the male among them has the like of the portion of two females. Included in this are the children

and the sons' children, by agreement of the scholars. Whenever the children, as brothers and sisters, are together, they divide the inheritance in this way according to most scholars. So if there is one daughter of the deceased's own body, or two, and also a son's son together with his sister, the two of them divide the remainder in thirds,
since they fall within this general rule.
This is the view of the majority of scholars, among them ʿUmar, ʿAlī, Zayd and Ibn ʿAbbās; the general body of scholars and the four imams adopted it.

Ibn Masʿūd held that what remains after the direct daughters have taken their full two-thirds goes entirely to the son's son, and that he does not make his sister an agnatic heir with him. This is the view of ʿAlqamah, Abū Thawr and the Ẓāhirīs.

On their view a child does not make his sister an agnatic heir unless she would have a fixed share if she were without him. Accordingly they said, where there is a daughter and a son's children, male and female, that the remainder goes to all of the son's children, the male among them having the like of the portion of two females.

Ibn Masʿūd said, concerning a daughter, son's daughters and son's sons: The daughter has half, and the remainder goes to the son's children, the male having the like of the portion of two females — unless dividing it this way would give the son's daughters more than a sixth, in which case a sixth is assigned to them and the rest is given to the son's sons. This is the view of Abū Thawr.

The majority said: The remaining half goes to the son's children, the male having the like of the portion of two females, acting on the general sense of the verse. In their view a child, however far down, makes those on his own level agnatic heirs in every case,

whether or not the female would have a share without him; he makes the females above him agnatic heirs only on condition that they have no share without him; and he never makes those below him agnatic heirs.
Then the Exalted says: “If they are women, more than two, they have two-thirds of what he left; and if there is one, she has half” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11].

This is the ruling when the female children are on their own: a single one has half, and more than two have two-thirds. Included in this are the direct daughters, and the son's daughters when there are no direct daughters. If both are present, then if the direct daughters have taken the full two-thirds,

the son's daughters on their own get nothing; and if the daughters have not taken the full two-thirds, because the direct child is a single daughter and there are son's daughters with her, the daughter has half and the son's daughters have a sixth, completing the two-thirds,
so that the share of the daughters does not exceed two-thirds. That is how the Prophet ﷺ judged in the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd mentioned earlier, and it is the view of the general body of scholars,
except for what is narrated from Abū Mūsā and Salmān ibn Rabīʿah, that the son's daughters get nothing; and Abū Mūsā came round to Ibn Masʿūd's view when he heard what he said on this.

The printed text names Ibn Masʿūd (عن ابن مسعود وسلمان بن ربيعة) as holding that the son's daughters get nothing. The same sentence goes on to say that Abū Mūsā came round to Ibn Masʿūd's view, and in the hadith in c9 it is Abū Mūsā who gives the son's daughter nothing while Ibn Masʿūd gives her a sixth; so read أبي موسى (Abū Mūsā), which is the reading of the Abū al-Nūr edition (the Arnaʾūṭ edition and Ibn Rajab's Tafsīr have أبي مسعود).

What puzzled the scholars was only the ruling on the inheritance of two daughters. They have two-thirds by consensus, as Ibn al-Mundhir and others related; and as for what is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, that they have half,
it has been said that its chain is not authentic, and the Qurʾān indicates otherwise, since He says: “and if there is one, she has half” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11]. How, then, could more than one inherit half?
And the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, in which the daughter is given half and the son's daughter a sixth completing the two-thirds, indicates all the more strongly that two daughters inherit two-thirds.
Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded from the hadith of Jābir that the Prophet ﷺ gave the two daughters of Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ two-thirds as their inheritance.

But it was hard to understand this from the Qurʾān, because of His words, Exalted is He: “If they are women, more than two…” That is why people were unsettled over this, and many of them put forward far-fetched views on it.

Some of them said: The ruling on the inheritance of two daughters is derived from the inheritance of two sisters, for the Exalted says: “If there are two sisters, they have two-thirds of what he left” [al-Nisāʾ 4:176]; while the ruling on the inheritance of more than two sisters is derived from the ruling on the inheritance of “more than two” daughters.
Others said: A daughter with her brother has a third by the text of the Qurʾān, so she has all the more right to a third with her sister. Others took another approach,

which is that Allah the Exalted mentioned the ruling on the inheritance of male and female children together, and the ruling on the inheritance of females on their own without males, but gave no text on the ruling when the males are on their own without females.

He made the ruling for them together that the male has the like of the portion of two females. If two or more daughters are together with a son, he has the like of the portion of two of them; and if there is only a single daughter with him,

he has two-thirds and she has a third. Allah called what the male is entitled to “the portion of two females” without qualification; yet two-thirds is not the portion of two females when they are together with a male,
since their portion in that case is a half. So two-thirds must be their portion when they are on their own.

There remains here a third category that the Qurʾān does not state explicitly: the ruling when male children are on their own. This can be brought under the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, “and whatever is left goes to the nearest male relative,” for this category has been left over, its ruling not stated explicitly in the Qurʾān,
and so the estate then goes to the nearest of the male children. The matter stands thus: if a son and a son's son were together, the whole estate would go to the son,
and if there were a son's son and a son's son's son, the whole estate would go to the son's son, in accordance with the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās. And Allah knows best.

Then the Exalted mentions the ruling on the inheritance of the parents, saying: “And for his parents, to each of them a sixth of what he left, if he has a child” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11]. This is the ruling on the parents' inheritance when the deceased child has a child,

whether that child is male or female, and whether a child of his own body or a son's child. This is something like a consensus of the scholars, though some have related a disagreement on it from Mujāhid.
So whenever the deceased has a child or a son's child, and has both parents, each of his parents has a sixth as a fixed share. Then, if the child is male,
the remainder after the parents' two sixths is his; and this may come under his words ﷺ: “Give the fixed shares to those entitled to them, and whatever is left goes to the nearest male relative.”

The nearest of the agnatic heirs is the son. If the child is female, then if there are two or more daughters, the two-thirds are theirs and nothing of the estate is left over; if there is a single daughter, she has half,

and another sixth of the estate is left over, which the father takes by agnatic right, acting on his words ﷺ: “Give the fixed shares to those entitled to them, and whatever is left goes to the nearest male relative.” For he is the nearest male relative when there is no son,
being nearer than the brother and his son, and the paternal uncle and his son.

Then the Exalted says: “But if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then his mother has a third” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11]. That is, if the deceased has no child and has both parents inheriting from him, his mother has a third; from which it is understood that the remainder after the third is the father's,

because He affirmed that his parents inherit from him and singled out the mother with a third of the inheritance, so it is known that the remainder is the father's. He did not say, “and the father has twice what the mother has,” lest it be imagined that they divide the estate by agnatic right, as children and siblings do when there are males and females among them.

The editions punctuate مثلاً in فللأب - مثلاً - ما للأم as “for example”. The argument (that the wording avoids suggesting the male takes twice the female's share, as in agnatic division) requires مِثْلا, “twice”, as in c62b (جُعل للذكر منهما مِثْلا ما للأنثى).
Ibn ʿAbbās held fast to this verse in his view on the two cases known as the two ʿUmariyyahs (al-ʿUmariyyatān): a husband and both parents, and a wife and both parents.

ʿUmar judged that the spouse takes his or her fixed share of the estate, and that in both cases the mother has a third of what remains after the spouse's share and the father has the rest; and the majority of the nation followed him in that.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: Rather, the mother has a full third, holding fast to His words: “But if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then his mother has a third.”
In reply to this it has been said that Allah gave the mother a third only on two conditions:

first, that the deceased child has no child; and second, that his parents inherit from him, that is, that his parents alone inherit from him. So long as his parents are not his only heirs, the mother is not entitled to a third, even if the deceased has no child.

It may also be said — and this is better — that His words, “and his parents inherit from him, then his mother has a third,” mean a third of what the parents inherit. He did not say, “then his mother has a third of what he left,” as He said in the case of the sixth.

The meaning, then, is: if he has no child and his parents have an inheritance from his estate, the mother has a third of that inheritance which belongs to the parents, and the rest remains for the father.

For this subtle reason — and Allah knows best — wherever Allah mentions the specified shares for those entitled to them, He says in them, “of what he left,” or something that indicates it, as in His words,

“after any bequest he makes or debt” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11], to make clear that the right of the one with a fixed share is that specified portion allotted to him from the whole estate after bequests and debts;

and wherever He mentions the inheritance of agnatic heirs, or what males and females divide among themselves by agnatic right, such as children and siblings, He does not qualify it with anything of that kind,
to make clear that the estate divided by agnatic right is not necessarily the whole estate: sometimes it is the whole estate, and sometimes it is what is left over after the specified fixed shares.
Here, when He mentioned the parents' inheritance from their child who has no child — their division of the inheritance being neither by fixed share alone, as in their inheritance alongside a child,
nor by agnatic right alone, in which the male makes the female an agnatic heir and takes twice what the female takes, but the mother taking what she takes by fixed share

and the father what he takes by agnatic right — He said: “and his parents inherit from him, then his mother has a third,” meaning that of the amount the parents are entitled to from his inheritance, the mother takes a third as a fixed share
and the father takes the rest by agnatic right. This is something Allah has opened up to me, and I know of no one who preceded me in it. To Allah belong praise and favour.

Then the Exalted says: “If he has siblings, his mother has a sixth, after any bequest he makes or debt” [al-Nisāʾ 4:11]; that is, with siblings the mother has a sixth of the whole inherited estate that the heirs divide.

He did not mention here the father's inheritance alongside the mother. There is no doubt that when a mother and siblings are together with no father, the mother has a sixth and the rest goes to the siblings; and according to the majority, two or more siblings reduce her share in this way.

If there is a father along with the mother and the siblings, most scholars say: The siblings reduce the mother's share but do not inherit. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that they inherit, as a fixed share, the sixth by which they reduced the mother, just as the mother's children inherit alongside the mother by fixed share.

It has been said that this rests on his view that kalālah is specifically one who has no child, and that kalālah does not require the absence of a parent; so the siblings inherit by fixed share alongside the father.

Some of the later scholars said: If the siblings are excluded by the father, they do not reduce the mother's share at all; she then has a third. The imam Abū al-ʿAbbās Ibn Taymiyyah (Allah's mercy be upon him) preferred this view, and it might be drawn from the general sense of the saying of ʿUmar and others of the Salaf:

One who does not inherit does not exclude. Aḥmad and al-Khiraqī said something similar. Most scholars, however, take that to mean one who is not fit to inherit at all, such as a disbeliever or a slave, and not one who does not inherit because he is excluded by someone nearer than him. And Allah knows best.

The view that siblings who are excluded do not reduce the mother's share might be supported by the fact that Allah the Exalted said, “If he has siblings, his mother has a sixth,” without mentioning the father,

which would indicate that this is the ruling when the mother is with the siblings alone, the whole remainder after the sixth then going to them. But this is weak, for the siblings may be maternal siblings, who have no more than a third. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Know that Allah the Exalted mentioned the ruling on the parents' inheritance but did not mention the grandfather or the grandmother. As for the grandmother, Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with them both) said:
The grandmothers have nothing in the Book of Allah. Some scholars have related a consensus on this, and that her share is established only by the Sunnah.
It has also been said that the sixth is a provision (ṭuʿmah) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted her, not a fixed share; this is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab.

It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, by routes containing weakness, that she takes the place of the mother when there is no mother and inherits the mother's inheritance, so that she inherits a third in some cases and a sixth in others. This is an isolated view, and it is not right to treat the grandmother like the grandfather,

because the grandfather is an agnatic heir related through an agnatic heir, while the grandmother has a fixed share and is related through one who has a fixed share, so her position is weaker. It has even been said that she has no fixed share at all, the sixth being only a provision the Prophet ﷺ granted her.

That is why a group of those who hold that any surplus is returned (radd) to those with fixed shares said that it is not returned to the grandmother, because her share is weak; this is a reported position of Aḥmad.
As for the grandfather, the scholars agree that he takes the place of the father in the situations mentioned earlier: with a child he inherits a sixth as a fixed share,

and when there is no child he inherits by agnatic right; and if something is left over alongside female children, he takes it by agnatic right as well, acting on his words: “and whatever the shares leave over goes to the nearest male relative.”

But they differed when a mother and a grandfather are together with one of the spouses. It is narrated from a group of the Companions that the mother has a third of the remainder, as when the father is with her, as mentioned earlier.

This is narrated from ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd — so some have transmitted it; others said that what is narrated from ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd is only that, in the case of a husband, a mother and a grandfather, the mother has a third of the remainder.

Another report is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd: that the remaining half is divided equally between the grandfather and the mother. As for a wife, a mother and a grandfather, an isolated report is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd that the mother has a third of the remainder; but what is authentically reported from him

agrees with the view of the majority: that she has a full third. This resembles Ibn Sīrīn's distinction regarding the mother with the father: if there is a husband with them, the mother has a third of the remainder, and if there is a wife with them, the mother has a third.

The majority of scholars hold that the mother has a third with the grandfather in all cases; this is the view of ʿAlī, Zayd and Ibn ʿAbbās. The difference between the mother with the father and the mother with the grandfather is that with the father a single name covers them both,

and they are equally near to the deceased, so the male of them takes twice the female's portion, as with children and siblings. The mother and the grandfather, however, are not covered by a single name, and the grandfather is further away than the father, so he need not be treated as equal to him in this.
If the grandfather is together with siblings, then if they are maternal siblings, they are excluded by him,
since they inherit only in the case of kalālah, and kalālah is one who has neither child nor parent — except for an isolated report from Ibn ʿAbbās.

If they are paternal or full siblings, the scholars have differed over the ruling on their inheritance, early and late. Some excluded the siblings by the grandfather absolutely, as they are excluded by the father. This is the view of al-Ṣiddīq,

Muʿādh, Ibn ʿAbbās and others. They argued that the grandfather is a father in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and so is included under the term “father” in inheritance, just as a child's child is a child
and is included under the term “child” when there is no child, by agreement; that siblings inherit only in the case of kalālah, so the grandfather excludes them, as he does the maternal siblings;

All three editions read كالإخوة من الأب (“as the paternal siblings”), which makes no sense when the paternal siblings are the ones under discussion. Ibn Rajab's Tafsīr gives the same passage as كالإخوة من الأم, which the argument requires (c48: the grandfather excludes maternal siblings because they inherit only in kalālah); translated accordingly.

and that the grandfather is stronger than the siblings, since fixed share and agnatic right come together for him through one and the same line, so he is like the father. He then falls under the general sense of his words ﷺ: “and whatever is left goes to the nearest male relative.”

Others had the siblings and the grandfather share the inheritance. This is the view of many of the Companions and of most of the jurists after them, with long disagreement among them over how they are to share it. Some of the Salaf withheld judgement on their case and gave no answer about them,
because it was so unclear and difficult. Were it not for fear of going on too long, we would discuss this question at length; but that would make this very long indeed.
As for the ruling on the inheritance of full or paternal siblings, Allah the Exalted mentioned it at the end of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, in His words, Exalted is He:

“They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalālah. If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, she has half of what he left” [al-Nisāʾ 4:176]. Kalālah is taken from the lineage encircling (takallul) the deceased and surrounding him,

and that requires that there be no line of descent at all, either ascending or descending. His explicit mention, Exalted is He, of there being no child points all the more strongly to there being no parent,

because a child's relation to his parent is more evident than his relation to his own child; so mentioning that there is no child points all the more strongly to there being no parent. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq said: Kalālah is one who has neither child nor parent; and the majority of the Companions and of the scholars after them followed him.
This has been narrated as marfūʿ among the mursal reports of Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from the Prophet ﷺ;

Abū Dāwūd recorded it in al-Marāsīl. Al-Ḥākim recorded it through a narration from Abū Salamah, from Abū Hurayrah, as marfūʿ, and declared it authentic; but connecting it through mention of Abū Hurayrah is weak.

His words, “If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, she has half of what he left,” mean: if the deceased has no child at all, male or female, the sister then has half of what he left as a fixed share.
What this implies is that if he has a child, the sister does not have half as a fixed share. Then, if the child is male,

he has the better right to the whole estate, for the reason established earlier regarding the inheritance of male children when they are on their own: they are the nearest of the agnatic heirs, and they exclude the brothers, so how could they not exclude the sisters?

Moreover, the Exalted says: “And if there are siblings, men and women, the male has the like of the portion of two females” [al-Nisāʾ 4:176]. This includes the case where there is someone with a fixed share, such as daughters and others. If the male siblings are entitled to what is left over when they are with the sisters,

then when they are on their own they are entitled to it likewise, and with more reason. If the child is female, the sister here does not have half as a fixed share, but according to the majority of scholars she has the remainder by agnatic right; this, and the disagreement over it, have already been mentioned.

Suppose there is a son who does not take the whole estate, together with a sister — such as a son who is half free, according to those who give him half the inheritance, which is the school of Imam Aḥmad and other scholars. Is it to be said that the son here cancels half of the sister's fixed share,

so that she inherits a quarter alongside him as a fixed share? Or is it to be said that he becomes like a daughter, so that the sister becomes an agnatic heir with him, as she does with a daughter, but he cancels half of her agnatic right, so that she takes the remaining half alongside him by agnatic right? Both are possible, and the scholars of our school have two views on this question.

The editions, and the same passage in Ibn Rajab's Tafsīr, read كما تصير مع الأخت (“as she does with a sister”). The sense requires مع البنت (“with a daughter”), since it is with a daughter that a sister becomes an agnatic heir (c6, c52e); translated accordingly.
His words, Exalted is He, “And he inherits from her if she has no child,” mean that the brother takes the whole of his sister's estate if she has no child, male or female.

If she has a male child, the child has the better right over the brother without any difficulty, for he is the nearest male relative. If the child is female, the remainder after her share goes to the brother,
because he is the nearest male relative; but he does not then take the whole of her estate, as he does when she has no child.

His words, “If there are two sisters, they have two-thirds of what he left,” mean that the share of two is two-thirds, just as the share of one is half. All of this concerns the ruling when brothers or sisters are on their own.

As for the ruling when they are together, the Exalted says: “And if there are siblings, men and women, the male has the like of the portion of two females.” This includes the case where they are on their own;

and where there is someone with a fixed share, from among the children or others — such as one of the spouses, the mother or the maternal siblings — what is left over after their shares goes to the brothers and sisters, the male having the like of the portion of two females.

It is clear from what we have said that the existence of a child cancels only the fixed share of full or paternal sisters. It does not cancel their inheriting by agnatic right together with their brothers, by consensus, nor their being agnatic heirs on their own alongside daughters, according to the majority.

Kalālah, then, is a condition for the sisters' fixed share, not for their inheriting at all, just as it is not a condition for the inheritance of the males among them, by consensus. This differs from the mother's children: the absence of kalālah cancels their fixed shares, and when their fixed shares are cancelled, their inheritance is cancelled,

because they never have agnatic right, since they are related through a female; whereas the full or paternal sisters are related through a male, and so inherit by agnatic right together with their brothers by agreement, and on their own alongside daughters according to the majority.

Since the child cancels the fixed share of full or paternal siblings, but not their inheriting altogether without a fixed share, it may be said that Allah the Exalted specified only the absence of a child, in His words “leaving no child”, and did not mention the absence of a parent or father,

because that would have included the grandfather, and the grandfather does not cancel the siblings' inheritance altogether; they only share the inheritance with him, sometimes by fixed share and sometimes otherwise. On the view of those who say that the grandfather does not exclude the siblings — and they are the majority — this is clear.

All of this concerns full or paternal siblings on their own. If they are together, the agnatic heirs among the full siblings exclude all the paternal siblings without disagreement — even the full sister with a daughter, according to those who make her an agnatic heir, excludes them just as the full brother does.

The Arabic reads literally “by whom the full brother is excluded” (يسقط بها الأخ من الأبوين), in all the editions and in the same passage of Ibn Rajab's Tafsīr. Read as “by whom [the paternal siblings] are excluded, as by the full brother”, which the context and the law require.

In the Musnad, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah, from ʿAlī, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ judged that full brothers (aʿyān banī al-umm) inherit to the exclusion of paternal half-brothers (banū al-ʿallāt): a man inherits from his brother by the same father and mother, to the exclusion of his brother by the same father.

ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ judged that, in kalālah, the full brother has the better right to the inheritance, and after him the paternal brother. This too falls under his words (peace be upon him): “and whatever is left goes to the nearest male relative.”
The precise position on this is that whatever the Qurʾān indicates, even by implication, is not among what the fixed shares leave over;

rather, it belongs to giving the fixed shares mentioned in the Qurʾān to those entitled to them — such as children, male and female, inheriting what is left over after the fixed shares, the male having the like of the portion of two females, and siblings, male and female, likewise.

That indicates by implication that the male among them takes the remainder all the more when he is on his own; and it also indicates by implication that the sister takes the remainder with the daughter, just as she would take it with her brother,

and that no one more distant than she, such as the brother's son, the paternal uncle and his son, is given precedence over her; for if her brother does not exclude her, how could someone more distant than he exclude her?
All of this, then, belongs to giving the fixed shares to those entitled to them, and to dividing the estate among those entitled to fixed shares according to the Book of Allah.

As for those agnatic heirs who are not mentioned by name in the Qurʾān, such as the brother's son, the paternal uncle and his son, and who are included only in general statements such as His words, Exalted is He, “And those related by blood are nearer to one another in the Book of Allah” [al-Anfāl 8:75], and His words,

“For each We have appointed heirs of what parents and relatives leave” [al-Nisāʾ 4:33] — their inheritance depends on this hadith, I mean the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās. If the estate has no other heir but them, they take it alone, the nearest of them being given precedence, then the next nearest,

because he is the nearest male relative. If there are fixed shares that do not exhaust the estate — such as one of the spouses, the mother, the mother's children, daughters on their own or sisters on their own — the whole remainder goes to the nearest male among these.

That is why, if these were brothers and sisters to one another, the men among them would take it to the exclusion of the women — unlike children and siblings, whose males and females share in the remainder, or in the whole estate, by the text of the Qurʾān.

The hadith indicates only the inheritance of those agnatic heirs whose males inherit to the exclusion of their females, namely everyone other than children and siblings. This, then, is the ruling on the agnatic heirs mentioned in the Book of Allah and in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās.

As for those with fixed shares, we have mentioned the rulings on their inheritance, and none of them remains but the spouses and the maternal siblings. The spouses inherit by virtue of the marriage contract.

Since between spouses there is the same affection, love, mutual support and assistance as between relatives, their inheritance was made like that of relatives, and the male of them was given twice what the female has,
because the male is distinguished from the female by the further benefit he brings through his spending and protection.

As for the mother's children, they are not of the man's tribe or clan; in substance they are among his womb relatives. So Allah allotted a sixth to one of them and a third to a group of them, as a gift of kinship, and made their males and females equal,

since in life their males bring no more support and protection than their females, as happens among the people of a single tribe and clan; so He made them equal in this gift of kinship. That is why bequests to non-relatives were not permitted beyond a third; indeed, a third is a great deal in their case,
for they are more distant than the mother's children, so they ought not to be given more than the mother's children receive as a gift of kinship, but rather less.
Some have argued from his words, “and whatever is left goes to the nearest male relative,” that distant kindred (dhawū al-arḥām) have no inheritance,

since he gave a right of inheritance to those not mentioned in the Qurʾān only if they are the nearest male, and this ruling is specific to agnatic heirs and does not apply to distant kindred; for those who give inheritance to distant kindred give it to their males and females alike.

Those who hold that distant kindred inherit replied that this hadith indicates the inheritance of agnatic heirs, but does not negate the inheritance of others; the inheritance of distant kindred is taken from other evidence, and so it is an addition to what the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās indicates.
As for his words, literally “to the nearest man, a male (rajul dhakar)” — though a man can only be male — the correct answer is that rajul (“man”) is sometimes used
to mean a person, as in his saying, “Whoever finds his property with a man who has gone bankrupt…”, where it makes no difference whether he finds it with a man or a woman.

Qualifying it with “male” rules out this possibility and restricts it to the male, not the female, which is what is intended. Likewise with ibn (“son”): since it is sometimes used in a sense wider than male, as in ibn al-sabīl (“the wayfarer”), the ibn labūn (a camel in its third year) in the zakāh thresholds came qualified as “male”.
Al-Suhaylī has a discussion of this hadith that is laboured and extremely strained, with nothing of value in it; a number of those we have met refuted him on it. And Allah knows best.
